note: Vol. I No. 40. THE SEPTEMBER ORDINANCES ARE HERE: the board of trustees sat in Starr Foot's house on 1 September 1834 and shut the town's tippling houses and groceries on the Sabbath, under John H. Kinzie as president where T. J. V. Owen signed in July. Beside them the month's other two structural readings — the editor's count of 150 vessels discharged at the town's wharves since 20 April, and a lot on Lake Street sold with a large dwelling house and a well on it, one lot east of Haddock's Tavern. Pages 3 and 4 are the advertising pages and the segmenter alternates their columns line by line, so nearly every claim here names its own lines rather than a range.

The line is CUT down its left edge: the completions ('den', 'with the', 'it cargoes at') stand in issue page 2 COLUMN 5, where the segmenter put the other half of every line in this passage, and a locator cannot cross a column, so they are supplied in brackets here rather than quoted.

claims.notes: THE SABBATH CLOSING ORDINANCE, and with it the town's own count of what it was legislating against: 'any tippling house or grocery … whether the same be licenced under the name, and as a tavern or house of public entertainment or not'. The town of 1834 therefore held THREE things the ordinance had to name separately — the licensed tavern, the grocery that sold drink, and the unlicensed tippling shop — and a reconstruction that puts only taverns on its streets is short a class of building the corporation thought worth a statute. THE PRESIDENCY HAS CHANGED SINCE JULY: T. J. V. Owen signed the July ordinances as president (1834-07-30, claim c001) and John H. Kinzie signs these. Isaac Harmon is still clerk, as he was on 30 July; the printed 'I. Hanwoy' is a recognition-class error on a name the same paper set correctly five weeks earlier.
